tier_reason: The README table matches the claimed numbers and the benchmark code is public (benchmark/benchmarks.jl), with the CPU named (Core Ultra 7 155U). It falls short of A: the README run does not name its Julia version, and the C baselines (Cubature, Cuba) are prebuilt JLL binaries whose compiler and flags are stated nowhere. Numbers are first-party from one laptop, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table, ns per call (ratios derived from page data): 2D x^2+y^2: FTS quad 2153 vs Cubature h 5980 (2.8x) and Cubature p 9098 (4.2x), Cuhre 6.858e4. 2D exp(x+y): FTS avx 5720 vs Cubature p 3.861e4 (6.7x) and Cuhre 6.697e4; the adaptive FTS quad is 2.438e4, only 1.6x faster than Cubature p. 3D x^2*y^2*z^2: FTS avx 2.207e4 vs Cubature p 2.441e4 (1.1x); FTS quad 7.634e4 is slower than Cubature p. Endpoint-singular 2D 1/sqrt((1-x^2)(1-y^2)): FTS avx 1865 and quad 3660 vs Cubature h 2.832e7, the only C baseline that met tolerance; Cubature p (2433) and all Cuba methods missed it. Not a win: 3D exp(x+y+z): FTS quad 1.069e6 and avx 3.401e5 vs Cuhre 1.795e5 and Cubature h 3.17e5. The checked-in benchmark/results/timings_full.md comes from a different run with different numbers (e.g. 2D x^2+y^2: FTS quad 1576 vs Cubature h 2720, 1.7x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia (JIT, no flags). The README table does not name the Julia version; REPRODUCIBILITY.md names 1.11/1.12 for tests and 1.13 for figures, and benchmark/Manifest.toml is not in the repo (404). The C baselines are Cubature.jl and Cuba.jl wrappers over prebuilt JLL binaries; their compiler and flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: This is an algorithmic comparison (tanh-sinh against h/p-adaptive cubature and Monte Carlo), not a language one. Baselines are Julia wrappers around C libraries that call back into the Julia integrand once per evaluation, so the comparison mixes algorithm with wrapper and callback overhead. The 'FTS avx' rows are not adaptive: they rerun a precomputed rule at the N the adaptive FTS run had already found (benchmark/benchmarks.jl: 'FTS avx is run at the N inferred from adaptive FTS convergence'), which is an oracle grid timed against adaptive solvers; the largest smooth-case win (6.7x on 2D exp) comes from it. Several baseline cells carry '*' (tolerance not met: Cuba Vegas and Divonne on 2D and 3D, Cubature p on the singular cases), so their times are meaningless for those cases. The run is author-run on one laptop CPU with samples=3, evals=1. Cuhre and Cubature h are faster on 3D exp(x+y+z). The README table and the checked-in results/timings_full.md disagree (different runs). The headline plot (JOSS_paper/benchmark_summary.svg) compares against the fastest accurate method per case, which for 1D is a Julia package (QuadGK or FastGaussQuadrature), not a C baseline. The JOSS review badge is present, but publication status could not be checked because joss.theoj.org did not resolve; JOSS reviews software, not benchmark claims.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithm, not language. Double-exponential node clustering converges in few points on endpoint-singular integrands, where h-adaptive cubature subdivides heavily. Prebuilt node and weight caches and transcendental caching in 2D/3D help further. The avx rows skip adaptivity by reusing an N found in a prior run. The baselines also pay a Julia-to-C-to-Julia callback per integrand evaluation.

notes: Downgrade A to C. Shortcomings: C-library build flags and the Julia version of the README run are unstated, the comparison is of algorithms rather than languages, the avx rows use an oracle N against adaptive solvers, several baseline cells miss tolerance, and the run is first-party on a laptop. Metadata checked: GPL-3.0, 16 stars, last commit 2026-04-16, not a fork.

tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (benches/spmv.rs, benches/lanczos.rs, benches/lanczos_two_pass.rs, ffi/ wrappers, build.rs, spack.yaml). Compilers and flags for both sides are stated (rustc nightly-2026-04-14, opt-level 3, fat LTO, target-cpu=native; clang 22 at -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto), and so is the CPU (Xeon Gold 6418H, one pinned core). I re-derived every geomean ratio in the record from python/data/summary.csv.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The README states no speedup. Ratios below are geomeans of per-matrix time ratios from python/data/summary.csv (derived from page data). SpMV, Rust faer/csr against: Eigen CSR 1.12x faster (wins 19 of 28 matrices, per-matrix range 0.85-1.66), Eigen CSC 1.20x faster, PSBLAS CSR 1.02x (parity; faer wins only 13 of 28). oneMKL CSR is 1.24x faster than faer/csr (faer wins 4 of 28), and PETSc CSR is 1.23x faster (faer wins 5 of 28). One-pass Lanczos, faer_csr: 1.04x faster than Eigen CSR (8 of 15) and 1.21x faster than PSBLAS CSR; PETSc is 1.19x faster (faer wins 2 of 15). Two-pass Lanczos, faer_csr: 1.04x faster than Eigen CSR (10 of 15); PETSc is 1.22x faster.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly-2026-04-14: opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native. C/C++ wrappers: clang/clang++ from LLVM 22 with -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto (build.rs; no -DNDEBUG, and cc-rs never adds it). PSBLAS Fortran wrappers: gfortran 14.3.0 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ffat-lto-objects. PETSc and PSBLAS libraries are built by Spack with -g -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto (spack.yaml); PETSc is linked against oneMKL. OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, taskset -c 0, MKL linked as mkl_sequential.
corrections.license: MIT declared in the Cargo.toml license field only; the repo has no LICENSE file
corrections.caveats: The repo has no LICENSE file, only license = "MIT" in Cargo.toml, so usability stays reference (upstream faer is already catalogued). The Rust side is a CSR SpMV specialisation the authors wrote in their own faer fork (codeberg.org/lukefleed/faer, commit 009ac1eb pinned in Cargo.lock; codeberg was unreachable here). That is a tuned kernel set against stock library kernels. Two Eigen-baseline weaknesses (ffi/spmv/eigen.cpp, build.rs): the wrappers compile without -DNDEBUG, so eigen_assert checks stay on, and the product runs as '*(ctx->y) += A * x' without .noalias(). Under Eigen's default product-aliasing rule that may evaluate into a temporary vector every call (not measured). Either could explain part of the 1.12x Eigen gap. The outcome is mixed: Rust beats Eigen on geomean and is at parity with PSBLAS CSR, but loses to oneMKL and PETSc on CSR SpMV and to PETSc on both Lanczos variants; per-matrix ratios against PETSc range 0.54-1.47. The companion paper (arXiv 2606.19213) is a preprint and was not opened (arXiv blocked). The authors ran the benchmarks on one machine.
corrections.why_faster: Not established. The Rust kernel is a CSR SpMV specialisation in the authors' faer fork (not reachable here), compiled by the same LLVM 22 as the C/C++ side with fat LTO. The Eigen baseline is built without NDEBUG and called without noalias(). MKL and the MKL-backed PETSc stay faster, so there is no language-level win over tuned C.

notes: Confirm at A; all of the record's ratios check out against summary.csv. Shortcomings to record: a mixed result (loses to oneMKL and PETSc, parity with PSBLAS), Eigen wrappers built without -DNDEBUG and using y += A*x without noalias(), the Rust side being the authors' own tuned faer fork, a license declared only in Cargo.toml, and an un-reviewed preprint. Metadata checked: 4 stars, last commit 2026-06-18, not a fork.

tier_reason: The README and docs/benchmarks.md carry the claimed numbers, and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/suite/speed_*.py, with results JSON in benchmarks/results/), with the CPUs named. It falls short of A: the FAISS side is the Python faiss module, and its version, build and flags are stated nowhere (no requirements pin). The numbers are first-party, so the tier is C.

corrections.workload: Search speed: nearest-neighbour search over 100K normalised OpenAI text-embedding-3 vectors (d=1536 and d=3072), k=64, 1K-query batch, median of 5 runs, 2-bit and 4-bit, single- and multi-threaded, on one ARM and one x86 cloud VM (8 cells per bit width). GloVe d=200 appears only in the recall tables, not in the speed runs.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'searches them 4.4x faster than FAISS, at matching recall'; '4.4x FAISS FastScan at 4-bit and 2.2x at 2-bit, on ARM and x86'. README table: search 4-bit '3.8-5.1x faster across the eight cells (ARM 4.0x, x86 4.9x)', search 2-bit '1.8-2.5x faster (ARM 2.05x, x86 2.35x)'. Spot check: benchmarks/results/speed_d1536_4bit_x86_mt.json gives 0.127 vs 0.588 ms/query, 4.6x (derived from page data). Project-recorded losses: whole-file save 1.0-1.4x slower and load to first search 1.0-1.5x slower than FAISS.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust release build. x86_64 builds target x86-64-v2 via .cargo/config.toml, with #[target_feature]-gated AVX-512 and AVX2 kernels chosen at runtime (README). The FAISS version, build (pip wheel variant) and flags are not stated; the benchmarks/suite scripts import the Python faiss module and use the default OpenMP threads, or faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1) in the st scripts.
corrections.caveats: Not the same algorithm. turbovec runs a staged search: one bit plane scanned with a table kernel, a shortlist ranked on the lower planes, the best rescored exactly, so the first stage reads about a quarter of the 4-bit code bytes. The speed comparator, faiss.IndexPQFastScan(d, m=d, 4) with the default L2 metric and no refinement, scans every code. 'At matching recall' is not supported for the speed comparator. FastScan's recall is never measured, the recall tables compare against a different index (IndexPQ m=d/2, nbits=8), the speed runs use an uncalibrated index, and the README recall row reports the calibrated TQ+. Per docs/benchmarks.md, the calibrated index trails FAISS by 0.7 points at R@1 for d=1536 4-bit, and GloVe d=200 is the harder regime. The author ran it on cloud VMs; the FAISS version and build are not stated; timings include Python call overhead on both sides. The x86 kernel adapts FAISS FastScan's pack layout, nibble-LUT scoring and u16 accumulators. Vector search sits at the edge of the numerics-and-arrays category; the orchestrator may re-file it.
corrections.why_faster: Algorithm, not language. A staged bit-plane search scans only the sign plane with a nibble-LUT kernel adapted from FAISS FastScan, then ranks a shortlist on the lower planes and rescores it exactly, so far fewer code bytes are read per vector than in a full FastScan pass. AVX-512 (VNNI, vpermb), AVX2 and NEON kernels are selected at runtime.

notes: Downgrade A to C. Shortcomings: the FAISS version and build are unstated; the win is algorithmic (a staged bit-plane scan against a full FastScan scan with no refine); 'matching recall' is measured against a different FAISS index (IndexPQ nbits=8) and never against the timed FastScan; GloVe is not in the speed runs. Metadata checked: MIT, 17.4k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not a fork; not a wrapper of FAISS, so not a duplicate.
